question.problem: Find the maximum value of $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}-{x}_{2}^{2}$ given that $‖x‖=1.$
question.worked_solution:
First, notice that ${x}_{2}^{2}\ge 0.$ So, we have that

$$
-{x}_{2}^{2}\le {x}_{2}^{2}.
$$

As a result,  

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & ={x}_{1}^{2}-{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & \le {x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & ={x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall that $‖x‖=1$ is equivalent to ${x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}=1.$ So,  in turn, $Q(x)\le 1.$

So, the value of $Q(x)$ can be no greater than $1.$ But before we conclude that $1$ is the maximum, we need to find a vector such that $Q(x)=1.$

Notice that when $x={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{T},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & ={x}_{1}^{2}-{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & =(1)^{2}-(0)^{2} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, given that $‖x‖=1,$ the maximum value of $Q(x)$ is equal to $1.$
